title: The 'pay ratio' provision of the Dodd-Frank Act 2010 and presentation of the Paulo–Le Roux Index
central_claims: Executive remuneration divided by modeled intrinsic operating value measures remuneration relative to executive value added.
The index can guide governance and resource-allocation decisions using audited financial statements across firms and subunits.

source_manifest.title: The 'pay ratio' provision of the Dodd-Frank Act 2010 and presentation of the Paulo–Le Roux Index
source_manifest.finding: Defines a remuneration-to-intrinsic-value index and proposes governance uses; empirical surveys are future work.

source_manifest.title: Accounting for uncontrollable factors in executive incentive scheme designs
source_manifest.finding: Dhliwayo and Bussin explicitly note that the index treats uncontrollable factors as endogenous; their interviews examine other incentive-design approaches.

source_manifest.title: Hierarchical Pay Incentives and Firm Performance
source_manifest.finding: Cites the article for disclosure-policy motivation; its empirical pay-dispersion measures do not instantiate the Paulo–Le Roux formula.

source_manifest.title: Executive Compensation Disparities: Analysing Pay Ratios Across Global Retail Sectors
source_manifest.finding: Analyzes pay ratios in sixteen retailers and cites the article contextually; does not calculate the named intrinsic-value index.

answers.rationale: No independent test establishes that this ratio isolates executive-created value or improves governance decisions.
No independent calculation or reconstruction of the exact index was found in the later empirical papers.
Later studies analyze generic pay dispersion or incentive design rather than testing the index on a larger dataset.
The 2019 discussion raises uncontrollable-factor attribution; it does not provide an authoritative retention or rejection of the full index.
The proposed extensive empirical surveys and stakeholder calibration were not verified as completed.
Later remuneration studies cite the article, but substantive modification of its specific formula was not shown.
The three later teams offer contextual discussion; two independent direct applications or extensions were not established.
Neither the 2023 hierarchy study nor the 2025 retail study calculates remuneration divided by the proposed intrinsic valuation.
No review identifies the named index as enabling a research direction.
The 2019 paper contrasts its treatment of uncontrollable factors conceptually, but does not use the index as a tested baseline or reference construction.
No independent application demonstrates improved pay decisions or resource allocation from the index.
Use across divisions, projects or countries is proposed in the original but not independently demonstrated.
New pay-dispersion results rely on other measures; they are not shown to depend on this index.
No organization or regulator was verified as adopting the named index in an operational pay-setting process.
No independent fair evaluation establishes its claimed informational benefit over existing pay or performance metrics.
Later citations after 2019 discuss disclosure and pay ratios without verified substantive reuse of the index itself.
No post-August-2019 independent assessment validates the core executive-value measurement claim.
Follow-up citations occur in several years, but substantive follow-up of the specific formula in two years was not established.
No independent synthesis was found adopting this index as a validated or useful measurement instrument.
The retrieved newer remuneration literature does not explicitly demonstrate retained usefulness of this index alongside alternatives.

search_gaps: Full original and relevant later methods/discussion were accessible. Generic pay-ratio research is not evidence that the specific intrinsic-value formula was used.
The 2019 critique flags attribution of uncontrollable influences but does not empirically falsify all claimed uses. Absence of a retrieved adoption report is not evidence of nonadoption.
research.summary: The index attracted discussion of uncontrollable factors and contextual citations in later pay-ratio studies. Independent validation, formula reuse and operational adoption were not established.
